title: Geometric Interpretation
teaches: The determinant represents the signed area scaling factor of a linear transformation.
visual: A unit square with vertices at (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), and (1,1) is drawn in blue. Two basis vectors i-hat and j-hat are highlighted. The square smoothly transforms into a parallelogram defined by new vector positions. The area of the resulting parallelogram is shaded red and labeled with a numerical value.
narration: Imagine the determinant as a measure of how much space stretches or shrinks during a transformation. We start with a simple unit square, representing one unit of area. When we apply a linear transformation, this shape morphs into a parallelogram, and the determinant tells us exactly how its area has changed.

title: Orientation and Sign
teaches: A negative determinant indicates that the orientation of the basis vectors has been flipped.
visual: The previous parallelogram is shown. A reflection transformation is applied, causing the shape to flip across an axis. The label changes from a positive number (e.g., 2) to a negative number (e.g., -2). Arrows indicating the direction of i-hat and j-hat are shown reversing their relative clockwise/counter-clockwise order.
narration: But the determinant is more than just size; it also tracks orientation. If the transformation flips the plane, causing our basis vectors to reverse their rotational order, the determinant becomes negative. This sign acts as a crucial indicator of whether the 'handedness' of the space has been preserved or inverted.

title: Singularity and Collapse
teaches: A determinant of zero means the transformation collapses space into a lower dimension.
visual: The parallelogram is squashed until it lies entirely flat on a line (or becomes a point). The red shaded area disappears, and the label clearly displays '0'. The basis vectors are shown becoming collinear (parallel to each other).
narration: What happens when the determinant equals zero? The shape collapses completely, losing all its dimensionality. This signifies that the transformation is singular; information is lost because multiple input points map to the same output, making it impossible to reverse the process.

title: Computational Formula
teaches: The determinant of a 2x2 matrix is calculated as ad - bc.
visual: A 2x2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] appears on screen. The terms 'ad' and 'bc' are highlighted in distinct colors. An animation shows 'ad' growing while 'bc' shrinks, with the final result 'ad - bc' appearing as the area value of the corresponding transformed unit square shown in the background.
narration: Finally, we connect this geometry to algebra. For any 2x2 matrix, the determinant is simply the product of the main diagonal minus the product of the other diagonal. This formula ad - bc provides a quick computational check for both the scaling factor and the orientation flip we observed visually.
